title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
gist: A Harvard study of Jellyfish data on 700-plus software firms finds AI coding agents raise lines of code, commits and pull requests, but Jira issue resolution does not change significantly because human code review time balloons 49 percent. The researchers see little evidence that firms increase software output or cut employment.

insights.claim: Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton used Jellyfish analytics covering 300 million work events and over 700,000 employees at over 700 software firms from 2021 through March 2026.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Large sample of real firms makes this stronger evidence than vendor claims or surveys.

insights.claim: The researchers used a difference-of-differences regression comparing outcomes before and after each firm adopted AI coding assistants or agents at different times.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Staggered-adoption design supports causal reading of the effects.
insights.locator: To assess the impact of AI tools

insights.claim: Introducing AI coding agents raises total lines of code by 30 percent, commits by 20 percent and pull requests by 23 percent on average.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Confirms the raw code-generation boost that vendors market.
insights.locator: In terms of raw code being produced

insights.claim: Resolution rates for Jira-tracked issues and epics did not change significantly after AI introduction, with no shift in the size or complexity of those issues.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Extra code is not translating into more delivered features, undercutting productivity-ROI claims.
insights.locator: In terms of raw code being produced

insights.claim: The study finds little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment by using AI coding tools.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Weakens the near-term narrative of AI replacing software engineers.
insights.quote: “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment”
insights.locator: A recent study of actual coding practices

insights.claim: Coding-phase efficiency gains are absorbed by downstream constraints, chiefly human code review, which acts as a bottleneck on the whole production process.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Value capture from AI coding depends on fixing review, not generation; tools targeting review may matter more.
insights.quote: “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”
insights.locator: A recent study of actual coding practices

insights.claim: Average time from pull request submission to merge rises 49 percent after AI agents arrive, the share of pull requests needing changes nearly doubles, and comments per pull request rise 35 percent.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Quantifies the hidden review cost of AI-generated code.

insights.claim: The share of workers performing code reviews increases 14 percent after AI agents are introduced, while the researchers cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Labor is shifting toward review rather than shrinking.

insights.claim: AI code review has so far had only marginal impact: although 80 percent of firms used it by March 2026, AI agents wrote only 23.3 percent of review comments and 10.8 percent of pull requests.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Automated review is widely adopted but not yet relieving the bottleneck, leaving a possible product opportunity.
insights.locator: While AI could also theoretically help

insights.claim: The study's data ends March 2026, agents have improved since, and 95 percent of firms have now adopted coding agents, so coding-versus-review trade-offs could improve as teams gain experience.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Results may be a snapshot of early adoption; re-test as tooling matures.
insights.locator: AI agents are still a relatively new part

insights.claim: Ars concludes that letting AI write code is a double-edged sword and wonders whether the time and expense of deploying coding agents is worth it for most companies.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Sceptical editorial view relevant to enterprise AI spending ROI debates.
insights.quote: It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.
insights.locator: For now, though, letting AI write your code
